code.title: struct vs class: only the default access differs

followUps:
An aggregate is a simple type you can fill with braces: no user-declared constructors, no private or protected non-static data, no virtual functions (and no virtual, private or protected bases). Arrays and plain structs qualify. struct Point { int x; int y; }; is one.

C++20 designated initializers name the fields: Point p{.x = 3, .y = 4};. The names must follow declaration order, so {.y = 4, .x = 3} is an error. Skipped fields get their default value (0 for ints). Using them with a class that has a constructor will not compile.

Yes, and it is very common. A struct can inherit from a class and the other way round, because struct and class are the same kind of type. Only the default access of the base differs: struct D : B {} inherits publicly, class D : B {} inherits privately.

class Base { public: int id = 7; };
struct Derived : Base {};   // public inheritance
Derived d; int v = d.id;     // fine, v == 7

If you write class Derived : Base instead, d.id would be inaccessible from outside.

code.title: Encapsulation protects an invariant

followUps:
No. Access control is a compile-time rule that helps honest programmers avoid mistakes; it is not a security boundary. Code in the same process can still reach private data with pointer casts, #define private public hacks, or by reading memory directly.

Real security needs separate processes, OS permissions or sandboxes. Think of private as a sign on a door that says staff only, not a lock. Its value is keeping the invariant in one place, so a bug is easy to find.

A public data member is fine when the type has no invariant, meaning every value of each field is valid and nothing else depends on it. A Point { double x, y; }, a settings record or a plain return struct with several results are typical.

Test: could a setter reject a value or update another field? If no, a getter/setter pair adds only noise. If yes (a Date with month 1 to 12), make it private. That is the Core Guidelines split: struct for plain data, class for invariants.

code.title: Construction and destruction order trace

followUps:
The objects already fully built are destroyed, but the object under construction never finishes, so its own destructor does not run. The exception propagates to the caller.

Example: a class has members A a; B b; C c; and the constructor of C throws. Then b and a are destroyed (reverse order) and bases are destroyed too, but ~X() is skipped. So hold resources in members such as unique_ptr, never as raw pointers in the body: a raw new before the throw would leak.

Globals and namespace-scope statics are destroyed after main returns, in the reverse order of their construction completing. A function-local static is constructed the first time control passes through it, and it joins that same reverse order.

Example: global G built before main, local static L built on the first call inside main. At exit L is destroyed first, then G. A static never reached is never built and never destroyed.

code.title: Initializer list vs assignment in the body

followUps:
A default member initializer is a value written next to the member declaration: int hits = 0;. It is used by every constructor that does not mention that member in its list. If a constructor does list the member, the list wins and the default is ignored for that constructor.

struct W { int a = 1; int b = 2;
  W() {}            // a=1, b=2
  W(int x) : a(x) {} // a=x, b=2
};

It keeps repeated defaults in one place.

A delegating constructor calls another constructor of the same class from its list, so shared setup is written once. When it delegates, it may not also initialize members in that list.

struct Box { int w, h;
  Box(int w, int h) : w(w), h(h) {}
  Box(int s) : Box(s, s) {}   // Box(4) gives 4 x 4
};

The target constructor runs completely first, then the delegating body runs.

code.title: this pointer: type in const member and chaining

followUps:
Technically it is undefined behavior, even if the function never touches a member. The standard says calling a non-static member function through a null pointer is UB, and compilers are allowed to assume it never happens.

It often seems to work, because this is just a null address that is never read. But an optimizer may remove later null checks, and a virtual call crashes at once because it reads the vtable pointer. If the function does not need an object, make it static.

C++23 "deducing this" lets a member function declare the object as an explicit first parameter: void f(this Self&& self). The compiler deduces the type, so one function can serve const, non-const, lvalue and rvalue objects without writing four overloads.

struct S { int v;
  auto& get(this auto&& self) { return self.v; }
};

It also makes recursive lambdas and CRTP simpler. Plain this is not a pointer in that form; you use the named parameter.

code.title: Static data members and static functions

followUps:
Because counter++ is three steps (read, add, write), and two threads can interleave them and lose an update. That is a data race, which is undefined behavior in C++.

Example: the value is 5, thread A and B both read 5, both write 6. Two increments, result 6, not 7. Fix it with static std::atomic<int> counter; and counter.fetch_add(1), or guard it with a mutex.

It is a bug where a global or static object in one .cpp file uses another global from a different .cpp file before that one has been constructed. The order across files is unspecified, so the code may work on one build and crash on another.

Fix: use a function-local static (the Meyers pattern), which is built on first use: static Registry& reg() { static Registry r; return r; }. In C++20, constinit guarantees compile-time initialization for simple values.

code.title: Static member needs a definition (inline static)

followUps:
An inline variable (C++17) is a variable that may be defined in more than one translation unit, as long as every definition is identical. The linker keeps one copy and all files share it. That is why header-only code can now hold globals and static members.

// config.h
inline int maxUsers = 100;
struct S { inline static int n = 0; };

Without inline, including that header in two .cpp files gives a multiple-definition link error.

constinit (C++20) forces a variable with static storage to be initialized at compile time, but unlike constexpr the variable can be changed later. If the initializer is not a constant expression, the code fails to compile.

constinit int counter = 10;   // ok, still mutable
void f() { counter++; }

It removes the static initialization order problem for that variable, since no run-time constructor can run too late.

code.title: Access after public, protected and private inheritance

followUps:
Choose private inheritance when you need to override a virtual function of a base, or access its protected members, but the derived class is not truly a kind of that base. Composition (a member) cannot do either of those.

Example: class Stack : private std::vector<int> reuses the vector but hides its API. For everything else, a member is simpler: std::vector<int> items;. Private inheritance is also used for the empty base optimization with stateless policy classes.

The Liskov Substitution Principle says code written for a base class must keep working when given any derived object. A derived type must honor the base's promises: accept at least what the base accepts and guarantee at least what it guarantees.

Classic breakage: Square derived from Rectangle. Code that does r.setWidth(4); r.setHeight(5); expects area 20, but a square forces both sides equal and gives 25. Public inheritance should only be used when this holds.

code.title: Passing arguments to a base class constructor

followUps:
Delegation is inside one class: a constructor hands the work to another constructor of the same class, Box(int s) : Box(s, s) {}. Inheritance of constructors (using Base::Base;) makes the derived class accept the base's constructor signatures without you writing them.

Inherited constructors build the base with those arguments and then initialize the derived members from their default member initializers. They do not set derived members from the arguments, so add defaults like int extra = 0;.

The base subobject is built first, using the base constructor. A const member that belongs to the base was already given its one value there, and a const object can never be assigned afterwards. The derived class also cannot reach private base members at all.

If you want a different value, pass it to the base constructor: Derived(int v) : Base(v) {}. That is the one place the base const member can be set, since it is the base's own initializer list that does it.

code.title: Name hiding and using-declaration

followUps:
Yes, override turns an accidental hide into a compile error. If you write override and no base virtual function has exactly that signature, the compiler rejects it. Without it, a typo like void foo(int) const versus void foo(int) silently creates a new, unrelated function that hides the base one.

struct B { virtual void f(int); };
struct D : B { void f(long) override; };  // error: no match

It also works with -Woverloaded-virtual warnings.

Yes. A data member in the derived class with the same name hides the base member; both exist in memory, and the base one is still reachable as Base::x. The types can differ, because lookup looks only at names.

struct B { int x = 1; };
struct D : B { int x = 2; };
D d;  d.x;     // 2
      d.B::x;  // 1

The object holds two ints. Avoid it, since it confuses readers.

code.title: friend function and operator<<

followUps:
A hidden friend is a friend function defined inside the class body. It is not a member and is not visible to normal lookup; it is found only through argument-dependent lookup (ADL), meaning when one of the arguments has that class type.

class P { int v;
  friend bool operator==(const P& a, const P& b) { return a.v == b.v; }
};

That keeps the global namespace clean, speeds compilation, and avoids ambiguous overloads. It also allows implicit conversions on both operands.

The passkey idiom lets a class give access to just one function, instead of making a whole class a friend. A tiny type with a private constructor is the key, and only its friend can create one.

class Key { friend class Factory; Key() {} };
class Widget { public:
  Widget(Key) {}   // only Factory can make a Key
};

Anyone can call Widget(Key), but only code that can build a Key compiles, so access is narrow and checked at compile time.

code.title: 2 + x fails with a member operator+, works as a hidden friend

followUps:
Four operators must be members: assignment =, subscript [], call () and arrow ->. The language requires this so the left operand is always an object of your class, which stops odd conversions on it.

Everything else can be either. Rule of thumb: operators that change the object (+=, ++) are members; symmetric ones (+, ==, <<) are non-members or hidden friends.

C++20 lets you write operator== once and the compiler also supplies !=, and rewrites a == b as b == a when needed. Write operator<=> (or default it) and you get <, <=, >, >= too.

struct V { int a, b;
  auto operator<=>(const V&) const = default;
  bool operator==(const V&) const = default;
};

Six comparison functions collapse into two lines.

code.title: sizeof of empty classes and empty base optimization

followUps:
Put the largest-aligned members first and the smallest last, because each member is padded to its own alignment and the whole struct to its biggest member. char, int, char takes 12 bytes (1 + 3 pad + 4 + 1 + 3 pad); int, char, char takes 8 (4 + 1 + 1 + 2 pad).

struct A { char a; int b; char c; };  // 12
struct B { int b; char a; char c; };  // 8

Sorting by size, descending, is a good default. It matters when you store millions of objects.

Two different subobjects of the same type must have different addresses, since the language guarantees that distinct objects of the same type can be told apart by address. If a class had two bases of the same empty type, such as struct D : E, F where both derive from Empty, the two Empty subobjects would collide at offset 0.

So the compiler must give one of them a nonzero offset and the optimization is not applied to it. Different empty types can share one address, since they are different types.

code.title: Class with unique IDs and a live-instance counter

followUps:
A per-process counter cannot be unique across machines, so combine parts that cannot collide. Typical choices: a random 128-bit UUID, or a Snowflake style 64-bit value made of a timestamp, a machine id and a per-millisecond sequence number.

Example layout: 41 bits time, 10 bits machine, 12 bits sequence gives 4096 IDs per millisecond per machine, sortable by time. Or use a central service or database sequence that hands out blocks of IDs.

It is your design choice, but the usual answer is that a moved-from object is still alive, because its destructor will still run and decrement the counter. If you decrement in the destructor, you must count every constructed object, including moved-to ones, or the count goes wrong.

Simple rule: every constructor increments, the destructor decrements. A move constructor then either takes over the ID (the source gets 0 or a marker) or gets a new one. Pick one and document it.
